stem: Which Azure database is a globally distributed NoSQL service?
choices: Azure Cosmos DB
Azure SQL Managed Instance
Azure Files
Azure DNS
explanation: Cosmos DB is the globally distributed NoSQL database. SQL Managed Instance is relational, Files is file shares, and DNS resolves names.

stem: Which in-memory service caches data for fast reads?
choices: Azure Managed Redis
Azure Blob Storage
Azure DNS
Azure Policy
explanation: Redis is the in-memory cache. Blob Storage is durable object storage, DNS resolves names, and Policy governs resources.

stem: Which managed relational database supports the pgvector extension for embeddings?
choices: Azure Database for PostgreSQL
Azure Files
Azure DNS
Azure CDN
explanation: PostgreSQL supports pgvector for vector search. Files stores file shares, DNS resolves names, and the CDN caches content.

stem: What does a vector search find?
choices: Items most similar in meaning to a query
Items with an exact matching id
The newest item by timestamp
The largest item by size
explanation: Vector search ranks items by semantic similarity. Exact id, newest, and largest are lookups that ignore meaning.

stem: In Cosmos DB, what does the partition key control?
choices: How data is distributed across partitions
The encryption algorithm
The backup schedule
The firewall rules
explanation: The partition key determines how items spread across physical partitions. Encryption, backups, and firewall are configured separately.

stem: Which Cosmos DB consistency level gives the lowest latency and cost?
choices: Eventual
Strong
Bounded staleness
Session
explanation: Eventual is the cheapest and fastest, with the weakest guarantee. Strong and bounded staleness cost more, and session sits in between.

stem: What is stored in Azure Managed Redis to speed up repeated reads?
choices: Cached copies of frequently read values
The only copy of the system of record
Long-term audit logs
Container images
explanation: Redis caches frequently read values in memory. Redis is a cache, not the system of record, an audit store, or an image registry.

stem: In Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL, which value determines the logical partition where an item is placed?
choices: The item ID
The _etag value
The partition key value
The _ts timestamp
explanation: The partition key value assigned to each item determines which logical partition the item belongs to; all items with the same partition key value live in the same logical partition. The item ID uniquely identifies an item within a partition but does not determine the partition; _etag is a concurrency token and _ts is a system timestamp, neither of which controls partitioning.

stem: What is the maximum storage size of a single logical partition in Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL?
choices: 5 GB
20 GB
50 GB
100 GB
explanation: Each logical partition can store up to 20 GB of data, which is why a partition key with a wide range of values is important. 5 GB, 50 GB, and 100 GB are not the logical partition limit; 50 GB is the storage limit of a physical partition, not a logical one.

stem: In Azure Cosmos DB, a "hot partition" occurs when which of the following happens?
choices: Requests are spread evenly across all logical partitions
Each logical partition stays under 20 GB
The container has only one physical partition
A few logical partitions receive a disproportionate share of the requests
explanation: A hot partition arises when one or a few logical partition keys consume a disproportionate amount of the total throughput, causing uneven load and possible rate limiting. Even request distribution is the opposite of a hot partition; staying under 20 GB and having one physical partition are unrelated to whether a partition becomes hot.

stem: Adventure Works Cycles wants to choose an effective partition key in Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL. Which property makes the best partition key?
choices: A property that is the same for every item
A property with a wide range of possible values
A property with only two possible values
A property that is null for most items
explanation: A partition key with a wide range of possible values distributes data and throughput evenly across partitions, which supports horizontal scaling. A value that is identical for every item, has only two values, or is null for most items concentrates data into few partitions and creates hot partitions.

stem: In Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL, all items in the same logical partition share which characteristic?
choices: The same partition key value
The same item ID
The same consistency level
The same Request Unit charge
explanation: A logical partition is the set of items that share the same partition key value. Item IDs must be unique within a partition, not shared; consistency level is an account setting and Request Unit charge varies per operation, so neither defines a logical partition.

stem: A Fabrikam Inc. container uses UserID as its partition key and has 1,000 unique UserID values. How many logical partitions does the container have?
explanation: Each distinct partition key value maps to one logical partition, so 1,000 unique UserID values produce 1,000 logical partitions. 1, 10, and 100 undercount the logical partitions; the number of logical partitions equals the number of unique partition key values.

stem: Hierarchical partition keys in Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL support up to how many levels?
choices: One level
Two levels
Three levels
Four levels
explanation: Hierarchical partition keys (subpartitioning) allow you to configure up to a three-level hierarchy for finer data distribution. One and two levels are below the supported maximum, and four levels exceeds the three-level limit.

stem: In Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL, what combination uniquely identifies an item within a container?
choices: The consistency level and the item ID
The partition key value and the item ID
The Request Unit charge and the item ID
The change feed mode and the item ID
explanation: Combining the partition key value with the item ID creates the item's index, which uniquely identifies it. Consistency level, Request Unit charge, and change feed mode are account or operation settings, not part of an item's unique identity.

stem: In Azure Cosmos DB, a Request Unit (RU) is best described as which of the following?
choices: A measure of the storage used by a container
A measure of the number of regions in an account
A measure of the number of indexes on a container
A measure of the resources consumed by a database operation
explanation: A Request Unit is a performance currency that abstracts the CPU, memory, and IOPS resources required to perform a database operation. RUs do not measure storage, region count, or index count; those are separate concepts unrelated to the cost currency for operations.

stem: In Azure Cosmos DB, approximately how many Request Units does a point read of a 1-KB item consume?
choices: 1 RU
10 RUs
100 RUs
explanation: A point read that fetches a single 1-KB item by its ID and partition key consumes about 1 Request Unit. 10, 100, and 1,000 RUs overstate the cost; a simple 1-KB point read is the baseline of roughly one RU.

stem: In Azure Cosmos DB, throughput is provisioned and measured in which unit?
choices: Gigabytes per second
Transactions per hour
Request Units per second (RU/s)
Queries per minute
explanation: Azure Cosmos DB measures throughput in Request Units per second (RU/s). Gigabytes per second measures data transfer, and transactions per hour and queries per minute are not the throughput unit Azure Cosmos DB uses.

stem: In Azure Cosmos DB, which operation typically consumes the most Request Units?
choices: A point read of a single item
A complex query over many items
Reading the account endpoint
Listing the databases in the account
explanation: A complex query that scans and processes many items consumes a variable and potentially much larger number of RUs than a point operation. A point read of a single item is the cheapest operation, and reading the endpoint or listing databases are lightweight control-plane actions.

stem: How can a developer find the number of Request Units consumed by a specific Azure Cosmos DB operation?
choices: By counting the items returned
By checking the partition key value
By reading the request charge in the response header
By reading the item ID
explanation: Every operation returns the RUs it consumed in the request charge response header (for example, x-ms-request-charge). Counting returned items, checking the partition key, or reading the item ID does not report the actual RU cost of the operation.

stem: The Normalized RU Consumption metric in Azure Cosmos DB is expressed as a value in which range?
choices: 1 to 10
explanation: Normalized RU Consumption is a metric between 0% and 100% that measures utilization of provisioned throughput. The metric is a percentage, so 0 to 1,000, 1 to 10, and negative percentages are not valid ranges.

stem: What happens when requests to an Azure Cosmos DB container exceed the provisioned Request Units per second?
choices: The container is automatically deleted
The consistency level is downgraded
The partition key is changed
The requests are rate-limited with an HTTP 429 response
explanation: When requests exceed the provisioned RU/s, Azure Cosmos DB rate-limits them and returns an HTTP 429 (request rate too large) response. Exceeding throughput never deletes the container, changes the consistency level, or alters the partition key; it only throttles the excess requests.

stem: Which Azure Cosmos DB consistency level guarantees that a read always returns the most recently committed write?
choices: Strong
Session
Eventual
Consistent prefix
explanation: Strong consistency guarantees that read operations always return the value that was last written and committed. Session, Eventual, and Consistent prefix are weaker levels that can return older values and do not guarantee the latest committed write globally.

stem: Which list shows Azure Cosmos DB consistency levels ordered from strongest to weakest?
choices: Strong, Bounded staleness, Session, Consistent prefix, Eventual
Eventual, Session, Bounded staleness, Consistent prefix, Strong
Session, Strong, Eventual, Bounded staleness, Consistent prefix
Bounded staleness, Strong, Eventual, Session, Consistent prefix
explanation: By order of strength the five levels are Strong, Bounded staleness, Session, Consistent prefix, and Eventual. The other orderings misplace the levels; Strong is always strongest and Eventual is always weakest.

stem: Which Azure Cosmos DB consistency level guarantees read-your-own-writes within a single session?
choices: Eventual
Session
Consistent prefix
Bounded staleness
explanation: Session consistency guarantees monotonic reads, monotonic writes, and read-your-own-writes within a single client session. Eventual and Consistent prefix do not guarantee read-your-own-writes, and Bounded staleness bounds lag by version or time rather than scoping to a session.

stem: Which Azure Cosmos DB consistency level is the weakest, offering the lowest latency?
choices: Strong
Bounded staleness
Session
Eventual
explanation: Eventual consistency is the weakest level; reads may return a subset of writes but offer the lowest latency and highest availability. Strong, Bounded staleness, and Session are all stronger than Eventual and provide more ordering or freshness guarantees at higher cost.

stem: Which Azure Cosmos DB consistency level guarantees that reads lag writes by no more than a configured number of versions or time interval?
choices: Eventual
Strong
Bounded staleness
Consistent prefix
explanation: Bounded staleness guarantees that reads are not too out of date, bounded by a configured number of operations (versions) or a time interval. Eventual has no staleness bound, Strong always returns the latest write, and Consistent prefix only guarantees ordering, not a staleness window.

stem: What is the default consistency level for a new Azure Cosmos DB account?
choices: Strong
Bounded staleness
Session
Eventual
explanation: Session is the default consistency level for a new Azure Cosmos DB account, balancing strong guarantees within a session with good performance. Strong, Bounded staleness, and Eventual can be selected but are not the default level for a new account.

stem: Which Azure Cosmos DB consistency level guarantees that reads never see writes out of order, returning some prefix of all writes with no gaps?
choices: Strong
Session
Eventual
Consistent prefix
explanation: Consistent prefix guarantees that reads return some prefix of all writes with no gaps, so updates are never seen out of order. Strong returns the latest write, Session scopes guarantees to a session, and Eventual can return writes with no ordering guarantee.

stem: What is the change feed in Azure Cosmos DB?
choices: A backup of the entire container taken nightly
A persistent record of changes to a container in the order they occur
A list of indexes defined on a container
A cache of frequently read items
explanation: The change feed is a persistent record of changes to a container in the order the changes occur, which consumers can process incrementally. It is not a nightly backup, an index list, or a read cache; it is an ordered log of item changes.

stem: Which Azure Cosmos DB change feed mode captures delete operations?
choices: Latest version mode
All versions and deletes mode
Incremental snapshot mode
Point-in-time mode
explanation: All versions and deletes mode records creates, updates, and deletes, including intermediate changes, in the order they occur. Latest version mode does not capture deletes; incremental snapshot mode and point-in-time mode are not Azure Cosmos DB change feed modes.

stem: Which change feed mode is enabled by default in Azure Cosmos DB?
choices: Full export mode
Archive mode
Latest version mode
All versions and deletes mode
explanation: Latest version mode is the default change feed mode, providing the latest version of each item from creates and updates. Full export mode and archive mode are not change feed modes, and all versions and deletes mode must be explicitly enabled with continuous backups.

stem: To read the Azure Cosmos DB change feed in all versions and deletes mode, what must be configured on the account?
choices: Strong consistency
A hierarchical partition key
A vector index
Continuous backups
explanation: All versions and deletes mode requires continuous backups to be configured, which creates the all versions and deletes change feed. Strong consistency, hierarchical partition keys, and vector indexes are unrelated requirements and do not enable this change feed mode.

stem: Which system function performs a vector similarity search in an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL query?
choices: StringEquals
ArrayLength
VectorDistance
DateTimeAdd
explanation: The VectorDistance system function computes the distance between a stored vector and a query vector to rank items by similarity. StringEquals compares strings, ArrayLength counts array elements, and DateTimeAdd manipulates dates; none perform vector search.

stem: What is the default distance function used for vector search in Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL?
choices: Cosine
Euclidean
Dot product
Manhattan
explanation: Cosine is the default distance function and works well for general text similarity with embeddings such as those from Azure OpenAI. Euclidean and Dot product are supported alternatives but are not the default, and Manhattan distance is not offered.

stem: Which of the following is a valid vector index type in Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL?
choices: B-tree
diskANN
columnstore
bitmap
explanation: diskANN is a supported vector index type in Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL, alongside flat and quantizedFlat. B-tree, columnstore, and bitmap are traditional relational index types and are not vector index options in Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL.

stem: In vector search, a vector embedding is best described as which of the following?
choices: An encrypted copy of the original document
A compressed backup of a container
A pointer to a physical partition
A numerical representation of data in a high-dimensional space
explanation: A vector embedding is a mathematical, numerical representation of data in a high-dimensional space where position reflects the data's characteristics. An embedding is not encryption, a backup, or a partition pointer; it captures semantic meaning as coordinates in vector space.

stem: Which practice does Microsoft recommend for vector search queries in Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL?
choices: Always disable the vector index before querying
Always include a TOP N clause in the SELECT statement
Always use strong consistency
Always query without an ORDER BY clause
explanation: Microsoft recommends always using a TOP N clause so the vector search returns a bounded result set and avoids unnecessary RU cost and latency. Disabling the index, forcing strong consistency, or omitting ORDER BY do not improve vector query efficiency and can hurt performance or accuracy.

stem: Which set of distance functions does Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL support for vector search?
choices: Cosine, Euclidean, and Dot product
Hamming, Jaccard, and Levenshtein
Manhattan, Chebyshev, and Minkowski
Haversine, Great-circle, and Vincenty
explanation: Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL supports Cosine, Euclidean (L2), and Dot product distance functions for vector similarity. The other sets list string or geographic distance measures that Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL vector search does not offer.

stem: When enabling vector support in Azure Database for PostgreSQL, what name is used in the CREATE EXTENSION command?
choices: vector
pgvector
embedding
pgai
explanation: Although the community calls it pgvector, the extension and binary name is simply vector, so the command is CREATE EXTENSION vector. pgvector is the project name, not the extension identifier; embedding and pgai are not the extension name to create.

stem: What capability does the pgvector extension add to Azure Database for PostgreSQL?
choices: Automatic table partitioning
Full-text search in 50 languages
Vector similarity search
Columnar storage compression
explanation: The pgvector extension adds open-source vector similarity search, letting PostgreSQL store and query embeddings. pgvector does not provide table partitioning, multilingual full-text search, or columnar compression; those are separate PostgreSQL features.

stem: Which data type does the pgvector extension introduce for storing embeddings in PostgreSQL?
choices: jsonb
vector
geometry
hstore
explanation: pgvector introduces the vector data type, used when defining a column that holds vector embeddings. jsonb, geometry, and hstore are existing PostgreSQL types for JSON, spatial, and key-value data, not for embeddings.

stem: Which pgvector index type uses a graph-based algorithm for approximate nearest-neighbor search?
choices: B-tree
GIN
BRIN
HNSW
explanation: HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) is a graph-based index in pgvector that approximates nearest-neighbor queries efficiently. B-tree, GIN, and BRIN are standard PostgreSQL index types not designed for approximate vector similarity search.

stem: What does Azure Managed Redis provide?
choices: An in-memory data store
A relational SQL database
An object blob storage service
An email delivery gateway
explanation: Azure Managed Redis provides a fully managed in-memory data store based on Redis, used for caching, session state, and similar low-latency patterns. It is not a relational database, blob storage service, or email gateway; those are other, unrelated Azure services.

stem: In the cache-aside pattern used with Azure Managed Redis, how is data placed into the cache?
choices: It is loaded all at once when the cache starts
It is never removed once written
It is loaded on demand only as needed
It is replicated from another Redis cluster automatically
explanation: In the cache-aside pattern the application loads data into the cache on demand, only as needed, on a cache miss. Cache-aside does not preload everything at startup, keep data forever, or rely on automatic cross-cluster replication to populate the cache.

stem: Which module must be enabled on Azure Managed Redis to support vector similarity search?
choices: RediSearch
RedisBloom
RedisTimeSeries
RedisGears
explanation: Azure Managed Redis uses the RediSearch module to provide vector similarity search, and it must be enabled when the cache is created. RedisBloom (probabilistic data structures), RedisTimeSeries (time-series data), and RedisGears (server-side functions) do not provide vector search.

stem: Northwind Traders wants to store shopping-cart and user session data in Azure Managed Redis for fast access. Which caching pattern fits this scenario?
choices: Content cache
Session store
Data cache
Job and message queuing
explanation: The session store pattern uses an in-memory cache to hold shopping-cart and user session data, which is faster than querying a relational database on every request. Content cache serves static page fragments, data cache offloads backend database reads, and job and message queuing defers long-running work; none target session data specifically.

stem: Lucerne Publishing needs to run a SQL query against an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL container from a Python app. What should you use?
choices: The change feed processor
The SDK query_items method
The bulk import tool
The Data Migration tool
explanation: query_items runs the SQL query from the SDK. The change feed reads changes, and the bulk and migration tools move data, not query it.

stem: Margie's Travel sees high RU cost because every property in a Cosmos DB container is indexed, though queries filter on two. What should you do?
choices: Increase the provisioned RUs
Change consistency to eventual
Index only the queried paths
Change the partition key
explanation: Trimming the indexing policy to queried paths lowers per-query RU cost. Raising RUs pays more, eventual consistency does not cut query cost, and the partition key is fixed.

stem: Nod Publishers runs a read-heavy Cosmos DB app where each user must read their own recent writes at low cost. Which consistency level should you use?
choices: Strong
Bounded staleness
Session
Eventual
explanation: Session gives read-your-own-writes at low RU cost. Strong and bounded staleness cost more, and eventual drops read-your-own-writes.

stem: Northwind Traders needs every read to return the most recent globally committed write, with no staleness. Which level should you use?
choices: Strong
Session
Eventual
Bounded staleness
explanation: Only Strong guarantees the latest globally committed read. Session, eventual, and bounded staleness all allow stale reads.

stem: Proseware, Inc. stores article embeddings in Cosmos DB for NoSQL and must return the articles closest in meaning to a query. What should you do?
choices: Detect changes with the change feed
Run an unfiltered SELECT and sort in the app
Use a composite index on text fields
Store embeddings and run a vector search
explanation: A vector search performs semantic similarity. The change feed, an app-side sort, and a text index are not semantic search.

stem: Relecloud must reindex a downstream store whenever items change in Cosmos DB, reliably and in order. What should you use?
choices: A timer that polls the container
A Time to Live setting
A change feed processor
A periodic large query
explanation: The change feed gives reliable, ordered detection of changes. Polling and periodic queries are unreliable, and TTL deletes data.

stem: Southridge Video needs a Cosmos DB partition key that spreads writes evenly and avoids a hot partition. Which should you choose?
choices: A region field with few distinct values
A high-cardinality user identifier
A boolean active flag
A date truncated to the day
explanation: A high-cardinality key spreads writes and avoids a hot partition. A region, a boolean, and a truncated date are low-cardinality and create hot partitions.

stem: Tailspin Toys stores embeddings in Azure Database for PostgreSQL and must return similar documents for the requesting customer only. What should you do?
choices: A pgvector search across all rows
A B-tree index and exact-match query
A full-text search filtered by customer
A pgvector search plus a metadata filter on the customer
explanation: Similarity plus a metadata filter returns results that are both similar and tenant-scoped. A full-scan search leaks other tenants, and B-tree or full-text are not semantic.

stem: Trey Research needs to reduce the latency of vector similarity queries in PostgreSQL. What should you do?
choices: Increase max_connections
Create an HNSW index on the embedding column
Add a B-tree index on a text column
Vacuum the table
explanation: An HNSW index cuts vector-query latency. Connection tuning, a text index, and vacuum do not speed vector search.

stem: VanArsdel, Ltd. sees throughput drop under many short-lived PostgreSQL connections. What should you do?
choices: Increase the compute tier
Add a read replica
Enable connection pooling
Increase the statement timeout
explanation: Connection pooling fixes throughput loss from many short-lived connections. Scaling up, a replica, and a longer timeout do not fix connection churn.

stem: Wide World Importers must choose a column type to store embeddings in PostgreSQL. Which type?
choices: jsonb
text
bytea
vector
explanation: Embeddings need the pgvector vector type for distance operators and indexes. jsonb, text, and bytea cannot use vector distance operators.

stem: Wingtip Toys repeatedly requests the same lookups and needs an in-memory store that expires results after a set time. What should you do?
choices: Store the values permanently
Cache the values in Redis with a TTL
Publish the values on a channel
Append the values to a Redis stream
explanation: Redis with a TTL is the in-memory cache with expiration. Permanent storage, a channel, and a stream are not a TTL cache.

stem: Woodgrove Bank must ensure Redis entries are not served after the source data changes. What should you do?
choices: Increase the TTL
Disable key eviction
Delete or update the key when the source changes
Move to a larger cache tier
explanation: Invalidating the key on source change keeps the cache fresh. A longer TTL, no eviction, and a bigger tier do not guarantee freshness.

stem: Adventure Works Cycles needs similarity search over vectors held in Azure Managed Redis. What should you do?
choices: Store the vectors in a sorted set
Store the vectors in a hash with no index
Publish the vectors on a channel
Create a vector index and run a similarity search
explanation: A Redis vector index enables similarity search. Sorted sets, plain hashes, and channels cannot do similarity search.

stem: Northwind Retail stores each order in an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL container partitioned by /customerId. A checkout service already knows both the order id and the customerId and must fetch a single order document with the lowest possible request unit (RU) charge and latency. Which read operation should the service use?
choices: A SQL query SELECT * FROM c WHERE c.id = @id AND c.customerId = @cid with enable_cross_partition_query set to true
A SQL query SELECT * FROM c WHERE c.id = @id with enable_cross_partition_query set to true
A change feed read filtered to the customerId partition
A point read with read_item, passing the order id and the customerId as the partition key
explanation: A point read is a key/value lookup on the item id plus partition key and is the most efficient read in Azure Cosmos DB, costing about 1 RU for a 1 KB item. A query that filters on id and partition key is still a query, not a point read, and consumes more RUs. Adding enable_cross_partition_query fans the query out further. The change feed streams changes over time and is not a mechanism for fetching one current document.

stem: Contoso Logistics runs a Python service against an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL container partitioned by /warehouseId. A frequently run query returns items for one known warehouse but is charging high RUs because it fans out to every physical partition. Which change to the query_items call reduces the RU charge the most?
choices: Set populate_query_metrics to true
Increase max_item_count so more items return per page
Pass the partition_key argument so the query is scoped to that single logical partition
Set enable_cross_partition_query to true
explanation: Supplying the partition_key restricts the query to a single logical partition, avoiding a cross-partition fan-out and lowering the RU charge. populate_query_metrics only reports diagnostics. max_item_count changes page size, not partitions scanned. enable_cross_partition_query explicitly allows the expensive fan-out this scenario is trying to avoid.

stem: Fabrikam Media writes large product documents to an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL container. Only two properties are ever queried, yet write RU charges are high because every property is indexed. The team wants to cut write RU cost while keeping those two queries working. Which indexing policy change is correct?
choices: Switch the indexing mode from consistent to none for the container
Exclude the root path /* and explicitly include only the two queried property paths
Add a composite index on the two queried properties
Increase the container provisioned throughput
explanation: Indexing cost correlates directly with the number of unique paths indexed. Excluding the root and including only the two queried paths reduces indexed paths and therefore write RU charge while keeping those queries served by the index. Indexing mode none disables indexing entirely and would break the queries. A composite index helps multi-property ORDER BY or filter+sort queries but adds paths rather than removing them. Raising throughput increases cost instead of reducing per-write charge.

stem: Adventure Works runs an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL query that filters on /status and sorts by /createdDate in a single query. The query fails asking for a specific index. Which indexing construct satisfies an ORDER BY across a filter and a sort property efficiently?
choices: A composite index on (/status, /createdDate)
A spatial index on /createdDate
Excluding /status from the index
A vector index on /createdDate
explanation: Composite indexes serve queries that filter and order across multiple properties. A composite index on the filter and sort properties lets Azure Cosmos DB satisfy the ORDER BY efficiently. Spatial indexes are for geospatial data. Excluding the property removes it from indexing and worsens the query. Vector indexes are for VectorDistance similarity search, not scalar ordering.

stem: Tailwind Traders wants Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL to automatically index any new property added to their evolving document schema, while still excluding a couple of large unused subtrees. Which include/exclude strategy meets this goal?
choices: Exclude the root path /* and include only the paths currently in use
Set indexing mode to none and rely on point reads
Remove both includedPaths and excludedPaths from the policy
Include the root path /* and add the unused subtrees to excludedPaths
explanation: Including the root path /* means new properties are indexed automatically, and listing the unused subtrees under excludedPaths keeps them out. This is the recommended strategy for evolving schemas. Excluding the root requires explicitly adding every future property, defeating auto-indexing. Indexing mode none disables all indexing. An indexing policy must declare /* as either an included or excluded path, so removing both is invalid.

stem: Litware Bank runs a web session in which a user updates their profile and immediately reads it back. The application requires that within that user's own session the read always reflects the user's latest write, with the lowest latency and highest availability among options that guarantee this. Which Azure Cosmos DB consistency level fits best?
choices: Eventual
Consistent prefix
Session
Strong
explanation: Session consistency guarantees read-your-writes, monotonic reads, and monotonic writes within a single session, and is the default level offering low latency and high availability while still guaranteeing a client reads its own writes. Eventual and consistent prefix do not guarantee read-your-writes. Strong guarantees the latest global write but at higher latency, lower availability, and double read RU cost, more than this per-session requirement needs.

stem: An architect at Proseware notes that a read-heavy Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL workload doubled its RU consumption after a consistency change, even though query volume was unchanged. Which consistency level, when configured, doubles the RU charge of every read while guaranteeing reads always return the most recently committed write globally?
choices: Session
Strong
Eventual
Consistent prefix
explanation: Strong consistency guarantees reads return the last committed write, and under strong (or bounded staleness) the RU cost of any read operation is doubled. Session, eventual, and consistent prefix do not double read RU cost. Only strong and bounded staleness double it, and among the options only strong also guarantees the latest committed value on every read.

stem: Wingtip Toys needs a consistency guarantee where reads can lag the latest write, but only by a bounded amount that they can express either as a number of versions or as a time interval. Which Azure Cosmos DB consistency level supports configuring staleness by operations (MaxStalenessPrefix) or time (MaxStalenessIntervalInSeconds)?
choices: Bounded staleness
Session
Eventual
Consistent prefix
explanation: Bounded staleness lets you bound how far reads can lag, configured either by a maximum number of operations (MaxStalenessPrefix) or a maximum time interval (MaxStalenessIntervalInSeconds). Session bounds staleness to a session, not by versions or time. Eventual and consistent prefix provide no configurable staleness bound.

stem: Fourth Coffee provisioned an Azure Cosmos DB account with the default consistency level set to Session. A developer wants a specific client to request Strong consistency for one operation. What is the outcome of requesting Strong on that request?
choices: The request succeeds and returns strongly consistent data
The account default silently changes to Strong for all clients
The request is downgraded to Eventual
The request fails because a per-request ConsistencyLevel override can only relax consistency below the account default, not strengthen it
explanation: A requested consistency level must match or be weaker than the level provisioned for the account. The ConsistencyLevel override can relax below the account default but cannot strengthen above it, so requesting Strong above a Session default is not allowed. It does not succeed, because you cannot strengthen past the account default with ConsistencyLevel. The account default is not changed by a single request, and the request is not silently downgraded to Eventual.

stem: Humongous Insurance stores multitenant event data in Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL. One large tenant exceeds the 20 GB logical partition limit when partitioned by /tenantId, but partitioning by /userId makes every per-tenant query a fan-out. They want per-tenant queries routed efficiently and room to grow beyond 20 GB per tenant. Which partition key design is correct?
choices: A single partition key of /userId
A single partition key of /tenantId
A hierarchical (subpartitioned) key of /tenantId then /userId
A synthetic partition key concatenating tenantId and userId as a string
explanation: A hierarchical partition key on /tenantId then /userId lets a single tenant exceed 20 GB across physical partitions, and queries specifying tenantId (or tenantId and userId) are routed to only the relevant partitions. A single /userId key makes per-tenant queries fan out. A single /tenantId key hits the 20 GB logical partition limit for the large tenant. A synthetic concatenated key adds complexity and still fans out for tenant-level queries unless every user is specified.

stem: A developer at Coho Winery is scripting creation of a subpartitioned Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL container with keys /TenantId, /UserId, and /SessionId. Which partition key definition values are required for hierarchical partition keys?
choices: kind set to Hash and version 1
kind set to MultiHash and version 2
kind set to Range and version 2
kind set to MultiHash and version 1
explanation: Hierarchical partition keys use a partition key definition with kind MultiHash and version 2, listing up to three key paths. Single (non-hierarchical) keys use Hash. Range is not a valid partition key kind here, and version must be 2 for MultiHash subpartitioning, not 1.

stem: A container at Blue Yonder uses a hierarchical partition key of /TenantId then /UserId then /SessionId. An engineer runs a query whose only filter is WHERE c.UserId = @u. How is this query routed?
choices: As a fan-out query to all physical partitions
To the single physical partition holding that UserId
To only the physical partitions holding that TenantId
It is rejected as an invalid query
explanation: Providing only a middle level of the hierarchy (UserId) without the leading TenantId cannot be prefix-routed, so the query fans out to all physical partitions. There is no single partition for a middle-only value. Efficient routing requires the leading key (TenantId), or the full prefix. The query is valid but expensive, not rejected.

stem: Graphic Design Institute has an existing Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL container partitioned by /region and now wants a hierarchical partition key of /region then /storeId. What is the supported way to make this change?
choices: Alter the existing container to add the second-level key in place
Add /storeId to the indexing policy of the existing container
Enable subpartitioning by setting version to 2 on the existing container
Create a new container with the hierarchical key and run a container copy job to move the data
explanation: Adding hierarchical partition keys to an existing container is not supported. You create a new container with the desired hierarchical key and use a container copy job to migrate the data. The partition key cannot be altered in place, the indexing policy does not define partitioning, and toggling the version on an existing container does not convert it to subpartitioned.

stem: Relecloud stores 1536-dimension embeddings from an Azure OpenAI model in Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL and needs low-latency approximate similarity search across millions of vectors. Which vector index type should they define?
choices: flat
quantizedFlat
diskANN
A composite index on the vector path
explanation: diskANN builds an approximate nearest neighbor index supporting up to 4096 dimensions and is designed for fast, efficient search at large scale. flat is limited to 505 dimensions and does an exhaustive brute-force scan. quantizedFlat is brute-force and recommended only up to about 50,000 scoped vectors. A composite index does not serve VectorDistance searches.

stem: A team at Margie's Travel stores 384-dimension embeddings for a small catalog of a few thousand items in Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL and requires guaranteed 100 percent recall (the exact nearest neighbors). Which vector index type meets this requirement?
choices: diskANN
flat
A geospatial index
No index, relying on autoscale
explanation: The flat index performs a brute-force exact search producing 100 percent recall and supports up to 505 dimensions, which fits 384-dimension vectors for a small dataset. diskANN is approximate and does not guarantee exact recall. A geospatial index is unrelated to vector similarity. Autoscale governs throughput, not recall.

stem: An engineer at VanArsdel writes an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL vector query using VectorDistance in the ORDER BY clause, and RU charges and latency are far higher than expected. Which correction most directly addresses this?
choices: Add a TOP N clause to the SELECT so only the closest N results are returned
Remove the ORDER BY VectorDistance clause
Switch the account to Strong consistency
Set enable_cross_partition_query to false
explanation: A vector search without a TOP N clause tries to return far more results than needed, increasing RU cost and latency. Always use TOP N with VectorDistance ordering. Removing the ORDER BY defeats similarity ranking. Strong consistency would raise, not lower, RU cost. Disabling cross-partition query can break a search that must span partitions and does not address the missing TOP N.

stem: A developer at Alpine Ski House provisioned an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL container without a vector index and now wants to add vector search to the existing container. What is true about enabling the vector index?
choices: The vector index can be added to the existing container at any time and later disabled
Vector search only works on containers using shared (database-level) throughput
A vector index can use a wildcard path such as /* to cover all properties
The vector index is immutable and must be defined at container creation time
explanation: The vector index is immutable and must be defined when the container is created; once vector indexing and search are enabled they cannot be disabled. It cannot be added to an existing container after the fact or later disabled. Vector search is not supported on shared throughput accounts, and vector policy paths cannot use wildcards or be nested in arrays.

stem: A data engineer at Trey Research must audit deletes in an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL container and process every intermediate update to an item, even when several updates happen between reads. Which change feed configuration meets this requirement?
choices: Latest version mode
A time to live (TTL) policy on the container
All versions and deletes mode with continuous backups configured
Latest version mode with a soft-delete flag
explanation: All versions and deletes mode records creates, updates, and deletes in order, including intermediate versions, and requires continuous backups to be configured on the account. Latest version mode omits deletes and can miss intermediate updates. TTL deletes data but is not a change feed audit mechanism. A soft-delete flag with latest version mode captures the flag update but still misses intermediate versions and native delete metadata.

stem: Fabrikam runs an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL change feed in latest version mode to replicate changes downstream, but hard deletes are never propagated. Without switching change feed modes, how should deletes be surfaced to the consumer?
choices: Enable Strong consistency on the account
Add a soft-delete marker property to the item on deletion and let TTL remove it later
Increase the change feed processor lease count
Switch the container to autoscale throughput
explanation: Latest version mode does not capture deletes. The common pattern is to update the item with a soft-delete marker (which appears in the feed) and set a TTL so the item is later removed automatically. Consistency level does not affect delete capture. Lease count only parallelizes processing. Autoscale changes throughput, not whether deletes appear in the feed.

stem: A team at Wide World Importers deploys the Azure Cosmos DB change feed processor across several compute instances for scale and resilience. Which component tracks progress and lets work be distributed and resumed across those instances?
choices: A separate lease container
The monitored (feed) container itself
The indexing policy
The vector embedding policy
explanation: The change feed processor uses a lease container to maintain state, distribute work across instances, and resume from checkpoints. The monitored container is the source of changes, not the state store. The indexing policy and vector embedding policy are unrelated to change feed lease coordination.

stem: An architect at Contoso is choosing change feed modes. They need to read changes going all the way back to the origin of the container at any time. Which statement about retention is correct?
choices: All versions and deletes mode has unlimited retention, while latest version mode is limited to seven days
Both modes are limited to the continuous backup period
Both modes have unlimited retention
Latest version mode has unlimited retention, while all versions and deletes mode only reads within the continuous backup period
explanation: Latest version mode retains changes for the life of the container (unlimited), while all versions and deletes mode can only read changes within the account's continuous backup retention period. The retention characteristics are reversed in the other options. All versions and deletes mode is bounded by the backup window, and latest version mode is not limited to seven days.

stem: Lamna Healthcare stores chat session documents in Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL and wants each document automatically deleted 3600 seconds after its last update, with no explicit delete calls from the application. What container configuration achieves this?
choices: Set DefaultTimeToLive to -1 on the container
Leave DefaultTimeToLive as null and set ttl on each item
Set DefaultTimeToLive to 3600 on the container
Set DefaultTimeToLive to 0 on the container
explanation: Setting DefaultTimeToLive to a positive value (3600) makes every item expire that many seconds after its last modified time, deleted automatically as a background task. -1 means items never expire by default. If the container DefaultTimeToLive is null, item-level ttl is ignored, so items would not expire. A value of 0 is not a valid TTL setting.

stem: A container at Woodgrove Bank has DefaultTimeToLive set to -1. A developer sets ttl to 600 on one specific item. What happens?
choices: The item never expires because the container TTL is -1
That one item expires 600 seconds after its last modification while other items do not expire
Setting item ttl is ignored because container TTL must be a positive number
All items in the container expire after 600 seconds
explanation: With container TTL set to -1, items do not expire by default, but an item-level ttl overrides that default, so the item with ttl 600 expires after 600 seconds while the rest remain. The item does expire because its item-level ttl overrides the container default. Item ttl is honored as long as container TTL is not null, including when it is -1, and only the overridden item is affected.

stem: An operations engineer at Munson's Pickles wants to completely disable TTL on an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL container so the background expiration process stops checking, even for items that previously set their own ttl. Which action is correct?
choices: Remove (set to null) the DefaultTimeToLive property on the container
Set DefaultTimeToLive to -1 on the container
Set DefaultTimeToLive to 0 on the container
Delete each item ttl property individually
explanation: Removing the DefaultTimeToLive property (setting it to null) turns TTL off and stops the background expiration process, and item-level ttl values are then ignored. This differs from setting -1. Setting -1 keeps TTL on with no default and still honors item-level ttl overrides. A value of 0 is invalid. Editing every item ttl is impractical and does not disable the container-level process.

stem: Southridge Video has an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL container with unpredictable, spiky traffic. During occasional spikes requests are rate-limited under the current fixed throughput, and the team does not want to manually adjust RU/s. Which throughput configuration is most appropriate?
choices: Standard (manual) provisioned throughput at the peak value
Standard (manual) provisioned throughput at the average value
Disable indexing to save RUs
Autoscale provisioned throughput with an appropriate max RU/s
explanation: Autoscale automatically scales throughput between 10 percent of the maximum and the maximum, absorbing unpredictable spikes without manual intervention, and is cost-effective when average utilization is below about 66 percent. Manual at peak wastes money during idle hours and still needs manual changes to move the ceiling. Manual at average continues to rate-limit during spikes. Disabling indexing harms queries and does not address spike handling.

stem: A team at Fabrikam sets an Azure Cosmos DB container to autoscale with a maximum of 20,000 RU/s. During an idle hour with no traffic, what is the minimum RU/s the system scales down to, and how is that hour billed?
choices: It scales to 0 RU/s and the hour is free
It stays at 20,000 RU/s and is billed at the full maximum
It scales to 2,000 RU/s (10 percent of max) and is billed at that level
It scales to 400 RU/s, the fixed autoscale floor
explanation: Autoscale scales down to 10 percent of the maximum. For a 20,000 RU/s max, the floor is 2,000 RU/s, and autoscale bills for the highest RU/s reached in the hour, which during idle is the 2,000 RU/s minimum. Autoscale does not scale to zero or bill nothing. It does not stay pinned at the maximum during idle. The floor is 10 percent of the configured max, not a fixed 400 RU/s.

stem: Contoso analyzed an Azure Cosmos DB container with steady traffic whose normalized RU consumption stays between 72 and 100 percent every hour. Which throughput choice is the more cost-effective and why?
choices: Autoscale, because it always costs less than manual
Standard (manual) provisioned throughput, because average utilization above 66 percent favors manual
Serverless, because steady workloads are billed per request
Autoscale, because the 1.5x rate is waived above 66 percent utilization
explanation: When average utilization across the month exceeds about 66 percent, standard (manual) throughput is cheaper than autoscale, whose per-RU/s rate is 1.5x the manual rate. Autoscale is not always cheaper and its 1.5x rate is not waived. Serverless suits intermittent low-traffic workloads, not steady high utilization.

stem: Nod Publishers is building a retrieval-augmented generation app on Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server with pgvector. They want an approximate nearest neighbor index with the best speed-recall tradeoff, and they need to create the index before bulk-loading data because loading happens continuously. Which index type fits?
choices: HNSW
IVFFlat
A B-tree index on the vector column
No index (exact search)
explanation: HNSW gives a better speed-recall tradeoff than IVFFlat and, unlike IVFFlat, has no training step, so it can be created on an empty table before data is loaded. IVFFlat requires representative data to train its lists, so building it on an empty table yields poor recall. A B-tree cannot serve vector distance searches. No index means exhaustive exact search with poor performance at scale.

stem: Fincher Labs uses pgvector on Azure Database for PostgreSQL and prioritizes fast index build time and low memory use, accepting somewhat lower query performance, on a dataset that is fully loaded before indexing. Which index and practice apply?
choices: HNSW, and create the index on the empty table first
IVFFlat with an ef_construction of 64
HNSW with a lists value of 100
IVFFlat, and load the data before creating the index
explanation: IVFFlat has faster build times and lower memory use than HNSW at the cost of query performance, and data should be loaded before creating the index so its lists reflect the data distribution. HNSW trades more build time and memory for better queries. ef_construction is an HNSW parameter, not IVFFlat. lists is an IVFFlat parameter, not HNSW, so those combinations are mismatched.

stem: A developer at Ashford Analytics tries to create an index on a pgvector column declared simply as embedding vector and gets an error that the column does not have dimensions. They also plan to store 3072-dimension embeddings. What are the relevant constraints for IVFFlat or HNSW indexing?
choices: The column can be indexed without declared dimensions if data is loaded first
The column must declare its dimensions, and IVFFlat/HNSW can index at most 2000 dimensions
IVFFlat/HNSW can index up to 16000 dimensions once dimensions are declared
Only DiskANN requires declared dimensions
explanation: To index a pgvector column it must have its dimensions declared, and IVFFlat and HNSW can index columns with at most 2000 dimensions, so 3072-dimension vectors need dimensionality reduction to be indexed. Dimensions must be declared regardless of load order. The IVFFlat/HNSW limit is 2000 dimensions, not 16000. The dimension requirement applies to indexing generally, not only DiskANN.

stem: After building an HNSW index in Azure Database for PostgreSQL, a team at Relecloud wants to raise recall for a specific set of queries in one transaction without changing the setting for the whole connection. Which parameter do they adjust, and how?
choices: Increase hnsw.ef_search using SET LOCAL inside the transaction
Increase lists using SET LOCAL inside the transaction
Increase probes using SET LOCAL inside the transaction
Increase m using SET LOCAL inside the transaction
explanation: hnsw.ef_search controls the size of the dynamic candidate list at query time (default 40). Higher values raise recall, and using SET LOCAL inside a transaction block scopes the change to that transaction. lists and probes are IVFFlat parameters, not HNSW. m is an HNSW build-time parameter fixed at index creation, not a query-time recall knob.

stem: A team at Datum tuned an IVFFlat index in Azure Database for PostgreSQL and wants to raise search accuracy at query time, accepting slower searches. Which parameter should they increase?
choices: ef_construction
m
hnsw.ef_search
probes
explanation: For IVFFlat, the probes parameter controls how many lists are searched. Increasing probes improves accuracy at the cost of search speed. ef_construction and m are HNSW build-time parameters, and hnsw.ef_search is the HNSW query-time knob. None of them tune an IVFFlat search.

stem: Coho Vineyard builds a RAG search on Azure Database for PostgreSQL that must return only documents in a chosen category and, within that category, the most semantically similar chunks. How should the query combine relational filtering with vector search?
choices: Copy matching rows to a separate pure vector database and search there
Store the category inside the embedding vector itself
Run a WHERE clause on the category column combined with ORDER BY on the embedding distance in the same SQL query
Use two unrelated queries and intersect the results in application code
explanation: Because pgvector stores embeddings alongside the relational data, a single SQL statement can filter on the category column with WHERE and rank by vector distance with ORDER BY, combining metadata filtering and semantic search efficiently. A separate vector database duplicates data and loses the colocation benefit. Categories cannot be meaningfully encoded into an embedding for exact filtering. Intersecting in application code is slower and unnecessary when SQL can do both.

stem: An engineer at Fabrikam wants to generate embeddings for text stored in Azure Database for PostgreSQL by calling Azure OpenAI directly from SQL, keeping the data in the database. Which extensions enable this, and what setup is required?
choices: Only the vector extension; no allowlisting is needed
The azure_ai and vector extensions, after allowlisting them via azure.extensions and running CREATE EXTENSION
The pg_stat_statements extension alone
The wal2json extension for logical decoding
explanation: The azure_ai extension lets the database call Azure OpenAI to create embeddings, and it is commonly paired with the vector extension to store them. Both must be allowlisted (azure.extensions) and installed with CREATE EXTENSION. The vector extension alone stores vectors but cannot call Azure OpenAI. pg_stat_statements is for query statistics, and wal2json is for logical decoding, neither of which generates embeddings.

stem: A serverless API at Wingtip opens many short-lived connections to Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server, and the server is hitting resource limits from too many Postgres backend processes. Which built-in feature best addresses this?
choices: Enable the built-in PgBouncer connection pooler on port 6432
Scale up to the Memory Optimized tier
Create an HNSW index to speed queries
Increase max_item_count on the client
explanation: Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server includes built-in PgBouncer on port 6432, which pools and reuses connections so many short-lived client connections share a small set of server connections, relieving the per-process overhead. Scaling up adds capacity but does not solve connection churn efficiently. An HNSW index speeds vector queries, not connection handling. max_item_count is a Cosmos DB client setting, unrelated to PostgreSQL.

stem: After enabling the built-in PgBouncer on Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server (default pool mode), a team at Proseware finds that SET search_path issued in one transaction does not persist for later queries on the same client. Why, and what is the recommended fix?
choices: PgBouncer is failing; restart the server to persist session settings
Session settings never work in PostgreSQL; hardcode the schema in every query
Switch PgBouncer to statement pooling to keep session state
In transaction pooling mode server connections return to the pool after each transaction, so use ALTER ROLE to set the parameter permanently or use a direct connection
explanation: The built-in PgBouncer defaults to transaction pooling, where a server connection is released after each transaction and a later transaction may use a different one, so session-level SET does not persist. Use ALTER ROLE for a durable setting or a direct (non-pooled) connection. This is expected pooling behavior, not a failure needing a restart. Session settings do work on direct connections. Statement pooling is even more restrictive and does not preserve session state; it also breaks multi-statement transactions.

stem: An engineer at Tailwind runs Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server on the Burstable compute tier and wants to enable the built-in PgBouncer connection pooler. What should they expect?
choices: PgBouncer works on Burstable exactly as on other tiers
PgBouncer requires the Flash Optimized tier
The built-in PgBouncer is not supported on the Burstable tier; they must move to General Purpose or Memory Optimized
PgBouncer only works with the vector extension enabled
explanation: The built-in PgBouncer feature is supported on the General Purpose and Memory Optimized compute tiers, not on the Burstable tier. Changing to Burstable removes the built-in PgBouncer capability. It does not work on Burstable. There is no Flash Optimized tier for PostgreSQL flexible server, and PgBouncer does not depend on the vector extension.

stem: Consolidated Messenger runs a high-concurrency vector workload on Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server and needs a high memory-to-CPU ratio so more of the HNSW index and working set stay in memory for faster transaction processing. Which compute tier is most appropriate?
choices: Burstable
Memory Optimized
General Purpose
Elastic cluster coordinator on Burstable
explanation: The Memory Optimized tier provides the highest memory per vCore (about 6.75 to 9.5 GiB), suited to high-performance, high-concurrency workloads that benefit from keeping more data in memory. Burstable is for intermittent low-CPU dev/test workloads and uses a CPU credit model. General Purpose balances CPU and memory (4 GiB per vCore) but offers less memory per core. Burstable does not support the built-in pooler and is not for production concurrency.

stem: Wide World Importers has a product catalog too large to preload into Azure Managed Redis. They want the application to read from Redis first and, on a miss, read from the source database and populate the cache. Which caching pattern is this?
choices: Cache-aside
Content cache for static templates
Session store
Write-behind logging
explanation: The cache-aside pattern loads data into the cache on demand: the application checks the cache, and on a miss reads from the data store and adds the value to the cache for later requests. Content cache is for static page fragments like headers and footers. Session store keeps per-user session state. Write-behind is a write strategy, not the on-demand read-population described here.

stem: An architect at Lucerne Publishing plans to use Azure Managed Redis as a low-latency vector database for a RAG app. What must be configured, and when?
choices: Enable the RediSearch module after the instance is created, using any clustering policy
Enable RediSearch on the Flash Optimized tier for best vector performance
Set the eviction policy to allkeys-lru so vectors are evicted under pressure
Enable the RediSearch module during provisioning, and use the Enterprise clustering policy with the NoEviction eviction policy
explanation: Vector search in Azure Managed Redis uses the RediSearch module, which must be enabled at provisioning (modules cannot be added later) and requires the Enterprise clustering policy and the NoEviction eviction policy. Modules cannot be added after creation, and RediSearch requires Enterprise clustering, not any policy. RediSearch is not available on the Flash Optimized tier. RediSearch requires NoEviction, so an LRU eviction policy is invalid.

stem: A developer at Fourth Coffee is defining a vector index in Azure Managed Redis with the RediSearch module. Which index types and distance metrics are supported?
choices: IVFFlat and DiskANN index types with only COSINE
quantizedFlat and diskANN index types with L2 only
FLAT and HNSW index types with L2, COSINE, and IP distance metrics
Only a single brute-force index with Euclidean distance
explanation: RediSearch in Azure Managed Redis supports KNN search with FLAT and HNSW vector indexes and the L2, COSINE, and IP distance metrics. IVFFlat and DiskANN are pgvector/Cosmos DB concepts, and quantizedFlat/diskANN are Azure Cosmos DB index types, not RediSearch types. RediSearch supports more than a single index type and more than one metric.

stem: A team at Adatum needs vector similarity search in Azure Managed Redis and is comparing tiers for cost. On which tier is RediSearch (and therefore vector search) unavailable?
choices: Memory Optimized
Flash Optimized
Balanced
Compute Optimized
explanation: RediSearch is available on the Memory Optimized, Balanced, and Compute Optimized tiers but not on the Flash Optimized tier, so vector search cannot run there. Memory Optimized, Balanced, and Compute Optimized all support RediSearch and vector search; only Flash Optimized does not.

stem: Blue Yonder stores document embeddings in Azure Managed Redis and needs queries that return the nearest vectors but only among documents matching a specific tenant ID and category. What should they store alongside each vector to enable this hybrid filtering?
choices: Metadata fields such as tenant ID, category, title, and source URL, so queries can filter and return source information
Only the raw embedding vector
A second copy of the vector in a different distance metric
Nothing extra; RediSearch infers tenants automatically
explanation: Storing metadata (tenant ID, category, title, source URL, timestamps, access-control fields) with each vector lets RediSearch combine KNN search with numeric, text, and tag filters for hybrid search and return source details. Storing only the vector leaves nothing to filter on. A duplicate vector in another metric does not enable metadata filtering. RediSearch cannot infer tenant boundaries without stored fields.

stem: Contoso wants to cut Azure OpenAI cost and latency by reusing a cached completion whenever a new user prompt is semantically similar to a previous one, using Azure Managed Redis. Which pattern is this?
choices: Content caching of static HTML fragments
A write-behind cache of prompts
Session store keyed by user cookie
Semantic caching using vector similarity search
explanation: Semantic caching stores completions as embeddings and reuses a cached response when a new prompt is semantically similar to a prior one, reducing LLM cost and latency, and relies on vector similarity search. Content caching serves static fragments by exact key, not semantic similarity. Write-behind is a write strategy. Session store keys by user session, not by prompt similarity.

stem: A team at Margie's Travel uses Azure Managed Redis as a cache-aside cache for a product catalog and must ensure entries do not serve stale data indefinitely after the source database changes. Which mechanism most directly bounds staleness of cached entries?
choices: Rely on the NoEviction policy to refresh keys automatically
Store the catalog in a RediSearch vector index
Set a TTL (expiration) on cached keys so they refresh after a set period
Increase the number of client connections
explanation: Setting a TTL (expiration) on cached keys bounds how long a stale value can be served: after the TTL elapses the key expires and the next read repopulates it from the source, a core part of the cache-aside strategy. NoEviction prevents keys from being removed under memory pressure and does not refresh them. A vector index does not address staleness of cached values. More connections do not affect data freshness.

stem: Contoso runs an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL container. A reporting query uses ORDER BY c.price, c.rating and consumes high RUs. Which change lets the query sort on both properties efficiently?
choices: Rely on the default range indexes that Cosmos DB maintains on each property
Create a spatial index that covers the price and rating properties
Define a composite index on (price ascending, rating ascending) in the indexing policy
Switch the indexing mode from consistent to lazy
explanation: An ORDER BY clause on two or more properties requires a composite index defined on those properties in the matching sequence and order. Default range indexes serve single-property ORDER BY and filters but cannot satisfy a multi-property sort. Spatial indexes serve geospatial ST_ functions only. Indexing mode controls when the index updates, not whether multi-property ORDER BY is supported.

stem: Adventure Works has a Cosmos DB query WHERE c.name = 'John' AND c.age > 18. They want a composite index to optimize it. How should the composite index be defined?
choices: Place the range-filtered property first in the composite index
Define the equality property first and the range-filtered property last
Add two range filters to a single composite index
Use the /* wildcard in the composite path so all properties are covered
explanation: For a composite index, equality-filtered properties must come first and the single range-filtered property must be defined last. Putting the range property first breaks the ordering rule. A single composite index can optimize at most one range filter, not two. Composite paths cannot use the /* wildcard.

stem: Fabrikam needs several item writes to succeed or fail together as one atomic unit in Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL. What is the key requirement for using a transactional batch?
choices: The operations can span any partition key values within the container
The batch must include a pre-trigger to enforce atomicity
Each operation needs its own If-Match ETag to be atomic
All operations must target the same partition key value
explanation: A transactional batch is scoped to a single logical partition, so every operation must share the same partition key value. Batches cannot span partition keys. Triggers are not required and in fact cannot run inside a transactional batch. ETags provide optimistic concurrency, not batch atomicity, which comes from the shared partition scope.

stem: Tailwind Traders submits a Cosmos DB transactional batch of 150 small operations that share one partition key, and it fails. Which limit is the most likely cause?
choices: A transactional batch payload cannot exceed 4 MB
A transactional batch supports at most 100 operations
A transactional batch cannot exceed 10 operations
A transactional batch must complete within 30 seconds
explanation: A transactional batch is limited to 100 operations, so 150 operations exceeds the cap regardless of item size. The payload limit is 2 MB, not 4 MB (4 MB is the max query response). The operation cap is 100, not 10. The single-operation execution limit is 5 seconds, not 30.

stem: Wingtip Toys wants to prevent lost updates when two clients replace the same Cosmos DB item concurrently. Which approach implements optimistic concurrency control?
choices: Send the item _etag in the If-None-Match header to block the update
Rely on the fact that a stale _etag returns HTTP 409 Conflict
Send the item _etag in the If-Match header; a stale value returns HTTP 412
Set the account consistency level to strong to guard the write
explanation: Passing the item _etag in the If-Match header lets the server reject a conditional write with HTTP 412 Precondition Failed when the value is stale. If-None-Match decides whether to refetch a resource, not to guard a conditional write. A stale ETag returns 412, not 409 (409 signals an id or unique-key conflict). Strong consistency governs read recency, not lost-update protection.

stem: Northwind runs a Cosmos DB container whose normalized utilization is about 85 percent of provisioned RU/s in nearly every hour of the month. Which throughput option minimizes cost?
choices: Standard (manual) provisioned throughput
Autoscale provisioned throughput
Serverless
Autoscale configured with a higher maximum RU/s
explanation: When average utilization exceeds 66 percent of the hours, standard (manual) throughput is cheaper because the autoscale rate is 1.5 times the manual rate. Autoscale saves money only when you use the max for 66 percent of hours or fewer, which does not hold at 85 percent steady use. Serverless suits intermittent spiky traffic. Raising the autoscale max does not change that steady high utilization favors manual pricing.

stem: Proseware configures a Cosmos DB container with autoscale and sets the maximum to 20,000 RU/s. What is the RU/s range the container scales within?
choices: It scales between 400 and 20,000 RU/s
It stays fixed at 20,000 RU/s
It scales between 2,000 and 20,000 RU/s
It scales between 100 and 20,000 RU/s
explanation: Autoscale scales between 10 percent of the configured maximum and the maximum, so 20,000 max scales between 2,000 and 20,000 RU/s. The floor is 10 percent of the max (2,000 here), not a fixed 400. Autoscale does not stay pinned at the max. 100 RU/s is the lowest possible autoscale entry point, not the floor for a 20,000 max.

stem: Relecloud issues millions of high-volume lookups that already know each item's id and partition key. Which read pattern consumes the fewest RUs in Cosmos DB for NoSQL?
choices: A query that filters on the item id
A point read by id and partition key
A cross-partition query
A query with no filter that takes the first result
explanation: A point read (key/value lookup by id and partition key) of a 1 KB item costs 1 RU and is the most efficient read. A query filtering on id is not a point read and costs more RUs. Cross-partition queries are the most expensive read pattern. An unfiltered query scans broadly and consumes far more RUs than a point read.

stem: Woodgrove Bank changes a Cosmos DB account from session consistency to strong consistency. What is the effect on the RU cost of read operations?
choices: Read RU cost is unchanged by the consistency level
Read RU cost is halved
Write RU cost doubles while reads stay the same
Read operations consume roughly twice the RUs
explanation: Strong and bounded staleness consistency roughly double the RU cost of read operations compared with relaxed levels. Consistency level does affect read cost. Stronger consistency increases, not decreases, read cost. It is reads, not writes, whose cost about doubles under strong or bounded staleness.

stem: Fourth Coffee needs an audit pipeline that captures every create, update, delete, and intermediate change to items in a Cosmos DB for NoSQL container. Which change feed configuration meets this need?
choices: Use latest version change feed mode
Use all versions and deletes mode, which requires continuous backups
Use latest version mode with soft-delete marker properties
Enable TTL so deletions are recorded in the feed
explanation: All versions and deletes mode records creates, updates, deletes, and intermediate versions, and it requires continuous backups to be enabled on the account. Latest version mode captures neither deletes nor intermediate updates. A soft-delete marker is an app-side workaround that still misses intermediate updates. TTL removes items but does not create a delete record in latest version mode.

stem: Lamna Healthcare uses the Cosmos DB integrated cache through a dedicated gateway. A specific read request sets MaxIntegratedCacheStaleness to 0. What is the effect?
choices: The request always serves from cache with zero staleness
The request uses the default 5-minute staleness
The request never uses the integrated cache
The request caches its result for up to 10 years
explanation: A MaxIntegratedCacheStaleness of 0 means the read never serves from the integrated cache, regardless of consistency level. A 0 value disables cache reads rather than forcing a fresh hit. The 5-minute default applies only when the property is not set. 10 years is the maximum staleness value, not the behavior of a 0 setting.

stem: Coho Vineyard must ingest millions of items into Cosmos DB for NoSQL with the .NET v3 SDK at maximum write throughput. Which approach is designed for this?
choices: Set AllowBulkExecution to true on the CosmosClient options
Wrap all inserts in a single transactional batch
Increase MaxItemCount on the query options
Loop the inserts inside a stored procedure
explanation: Enabling AllowBulkExecution on the CosmosClient groups concurrent operations into optimized batches for high-throughput ingestion. A transactional batch is capped at 100 operations within one partition key, so it cannot ingest millions of cross-partition items. MaxItemCount tunes query page size, not writes. Stored procedures run within a single partition and are not the scalable bulk path.

stem: Margie's Travel wants to generate vector embeddings directly from SQL inside Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server, calling an Azure OpenAI deployment. Which approach is correct?
choices: Install pgvector and call its built-in embedding generator
Enable the azure_ai extension and call azure_openai.create_embeddings
Use the azure_ai.translate function to produce vectors
Write a trigger that shells out to curl for each row
explanation: The azure_ai extension's azure_openai schema exposes create_embeddings, which invokes an Azure OpenAI deployment to produce vectors from within the database. pgvector stores and indexes vectors but has no embedding-generation function. azure_ai.translate calls Azure AI Translator for text translation, not embeddings. Shell-out triggers are not the supported mechanism.

stem: Alpine Ski House uses a DiskANN vector index in Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server and needs higher recall at query time without rebuilding the index. What should they adjust?
choices: Increase max_neighbors on the index
Raise hnsw.ef_search for the query
Raise the probes setting for the query
Set diskann.l_value_is higher for the query
explanation: l_value_is is the DiskANN query-time search list size and can be set per connection or transaction to trade latency for recall without a rebuild. max_neighbors is a build-time parameter that requires rebuilding the index. ef_search applies only to HNSW indexes. probes applies only to IVFFlat indexes.

stem: Blue Yonder finds that an HNSW pgvector index in Azure Database for PostgreSQL is returning lower recall than required. Which query-time change improves accuracy?
choices: Increase hnsw.ef_search before running the query
Increase the lists value on the index
Lower ef_construction on the index
Increase the probes setting
explanation: A larger hnsw.ef_search enlarges the dynamic candidate list during search, improving recall at the cost of speed, and can be set per connection or transaction. lists is an IVFFlat build parameter, not an HNSW setting. Lowering ef_construction reduces index quality. probes tunes IVFFlat search, not HNSW.

stem: City Power uses an IVFFlat pgvector index in Azure Database for PostgreSQL and wants more accurate nearest-neighbor results, accepting slower queries. What should they do?
choices: Raise probes so more lists are searched per query
Lower probes so fewer lists are searched
Increase the lists build parameter at query time
Set probes equal to the number of lists for best speed
explanation: Raising probes searches more of the inverted lists, improving accuracy while reducing search speed. Lowering probes reduces accuracy. lists is fixed at index build time and cannot change per query. Setting probes equal to lists becomes an exhaustive scan, so the planner stops using the index and the query is slower, not faster.

stem: Litware runs a web tier that opens many short-lived connections, causing connection churn against Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server. The application does not use prepared transactions. Which built-in PgBouncer mode maximizes connection scalability?
choices: Session pooling
Transaction pooling
Statement pooling
Disable pooling and raise max_connections
explanation: Transaction pooling returns the server connection after each transaction and is the default recommended mode for the built-in PgBouncer, scaling best for short-lived connection churn. Session pooling holds a server connection for the entire client session, scaling worst for churn. Statement pooling releases the connection after each statement and cannot run multi-statement transactions. Raising max_connections increases per-connection process overhead, the very problem PgBouncer solves.

stem: Graphic Design Institute needs its Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server to survive an entire availability zone outage with automatic failover and zero data loss. Which configuration meets the requirement?
choices: Add read replicas in the same region
Enable same-zone (zonal) high availability
Rely on automated backups and point-in-time restore
Enable zone-redundant high availability
explanation: Zone-redundant high availability places the synchronously committed standby in a different zone with automatic 60 to 120 second failover and zero data loss. Read replicas replicate asynchronously and are for read scale-out, not zero-loss failover. Same-zone HA keeps both servers in one zone, so a zone outage takes down both. Point-in-time restore is manual recovery with potential data loss and downtime.

stem: Munson's Pickles plans to use Azure Managed Redis as a vector database with the RediSearch module. Which instance configuration does RediSearch require?
choices: The Enterprise clustering policy with the NoEviction eviction policy
The OSS clustering policy for higher throughput
The allkeys-lru eviction policy
The Flash Optimized tier
explanation: RediSearch requires the Enterprise clustering policy and the NoEviction eviction policy. RediSearch cannot run under the OSS clustering policy. allkeys-lru would evict indexed data, so NoEviction is required. RediSearch is not supported on Flash Optimized; use Memory Optimized, Balanced, or Compute Optimized.
